title: When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?

paper.title: When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?
paper.abstract:
Abstract Model–harness co-evolution has emerged as a prominent paradigm for recursive self-improving (RSI) agents, jointly evolving their execution scaffolds and intrinsic capabilities.
We study the persistent yet often overlooked brain–body mismatch problem in this paradigm, where an evolving harness (body) demands behaviors its model (brain) has not learned or restricts capabilities it already possesses.
We introduce CoEvo-RSI , a RSI framework that advances model–harness co-evolution through agent-driven, bidirectional historical inheritance.
Drawing on a shared evolutionary archive and execution feedback, a meta-agent coordinates harness development from historical designs with model checkpoint selection or merging and subsequent adaptation under the selected harness, aligning inherited capabilities with evolving execution requirements to reduce brain–body mismatch.
Using only supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on its own rejection-sampled trajectories, CoEvo-RSI makes Qwen3.5-9B competitive with larger models across diverse vertical applications, including multi-agent failure attribution, role-aware text-to-SQL, and smart-home instruction following.
It surpasses DeepSeek-V4-Pro on TraceElephant ( + 14.16 +14.16 agent accuracy) and GLM-5.3 on HomeBench VM ( + 4.90 +4.90 success rate), underscoring the need for brain–body alignment and the potential of bidirectional historical inheritance to advance agent co-evolution. sections.heading: 1  Introduction
sections.text: An agent’s capabilities depend jointly on its brain —the language model that reasons and selects actions—and its body —the harness that defines its tool interfaces, action space, memory, and execution workflow ( Lou et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026c ) . Accordingly, progress has followed two complementary directions. Model training improves the agent’s learned policy through supervised learning, reinforcement learning, and self-distillation ( Xia et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026b ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . Harness optimization improves the surrounding system with the model fixed, through iterative modification of prompts, tools, and control flow guided by execution feedback ( Lou et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026 ) , or population-based evolution that generates, evaluates, and recombines competing harness designs ( Lee et al., 2026c ; Zhang et al., 2026h ) . These directions meet in model–harness co-evolution , where model training and harness optimization jointly adapt an agent to its task domain ( Chen et al., 2026c ; Luo et al., 2026a ) . Recent systems demonstrate the promise of this approach across tool use, mathematical reasoning, search-based question answering, and chess ( Chen et al., 2026b ; Chen et al., 2026d ; Kim et al., 2026 ) . A co-evolution round couples harness evolution with model adaptation. Starting from a model–harness pair ( 𝐇 t , θ t ) (\mathbf{H}_{t},\theta_{t}) , execution feedback 𝐅 t \mathbf{F}_{t} guides changes to the harness, whose requirements in turn shape the model’s next adaptation ( Chen et al., 2026d ) . As either component evolves, the harness’s execution requirements and the model’s learned capabilities can drift apart. In this setting, we first identify and formalize the brain–body mismatch problem : Problem Definition During model–harness co-evolution, a pair ( 𝐇 t , θ t ) (\mathbf{H}_{t},\theta_{t}) exhibits brain–body mismatch when the behaviors required by 𝐇 t \mathbf{H}_{t} diverge from those learned by θ t \theta_{t} , or when 𝐇 t \mathbf{H}_{t} restricts the use of capabilities already present in θ t \theta_{t} . The problem is to maintain their compatibility through successive rounds of harness-model co-adaptation. Figure 2 : Brain–body alignment in model–harness co-evolution. Left: Historical harnesses and checkpoints are recombined and adapted to resolve interface mismatch. Right: Step accuracy versus Turn-level Interface Mismatch Rate (TIMR; Section 3.1 ) for ten evolved versions per method, from a three-round run evaluated on the Who&When test benchmark. In plain terms, the model may struggle to operate its harness, and the harness may underuse its model’s abilities ( Figure 2 ). Consider two concrete examples. ❶ Interface mismatch. The model emits XML tool calls, while the evolved harness expects JSON, causing otherwise correct calls to be rejected. ❷ Capability mismatch. The harness introduces an active context management tool for deciding what information to retain, summarize, or discard. A model unfamiliar with these operations may use it poorly; a historical checkpoint θ i \theta_{i} already possesses the relevant capabilities and provides a suitable starting point for adaptation. On the harness side, a historical design 𝐇 j \mathbf{H}_{j} can supply an execution workflow suited to the model’s capabilities. These examples motivate selecting predecessors whose inherited behaviors and structures support further evolution. To address this challenge, we propose CoEvo-RSI , a framework for model–harness co-evolution through bidirectional historical inheritance . Its evolutionary archive 𝐀 < t \mathbf{A}_{<t} records earlier harnesses, model checkpoints, their development histories, and execution outcomes. Each round begins with feedback from the current pair. A Curator organizes this evidence, and harness editors browse the archive, choose their own historical starting designs, and develop offspring harnesses. For each offspring, the framework selects or merges historical checkpoints to form candidate model–harness pairs. Evaluation identifies a promising pair for model adaptation under its harness, and validation determines which pair advances to the next round. The resulting designs, checkpoints, and outcomes extend the archive. This agent-driven inheritance connects the two sides of evolution: harness design draws on accumulated structural experience, while model initialization draws on capabilities suited to the emerging harness. Their coordination makes brain–body alignment the organizing principle of the evolutionary process. Our contributions are: • Problem Formalization. We formalize brain–body mismatch in model–harness co-evolution and introduce the turn-level interface mismatch rate (TIMR) as an inexpensive diagnostic signal for observable interface violations. • Method Design. We propose CoEvo-RSI , which combines an evolutionary archive with bidirectional historical inheritance. Harness editors select historical starting designs, and model inheritance selects or merges checkpoints to support adaptation under the evolved harness. • Empirical Evaluation. We evaluate CoEvo-RSI across multi-agent failure attribution, home care, and SQL tasks, with co-evolved Qwen3.5-9B outperforming Qwen3.8-Max on Who&When Pro ( + 4.40 +4.40 agent acc.) and DeepSeek-V4-Pro on TraceElephant ( + 14.16 +14.16 agent acc.).

sections.heading: 2  Related Work
sections.text: Self-evolving agents improve through changes to external execution systems, learned model parameters, or both ( Gao et al., 2026 ; Guo et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . We organize the literature around these optimization targets and the reuse of historical components that connects them.

sections.heading: Recursive Harness Improvement.
sections.text: Early agent systems established how external organization can improve a model’s behavior: ReAct interleaves reasoning and actions, Reflexion retains verbal feedback across trials, and Voyager accumulates reusable executable skills ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Shinn et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) . Agent–computer interface design further shows how the operations exposed to a model shape its effectiveness ( Yang et al., 2024 ) . Subsequent work turns these hand-designed mechanisms into optimization targets, evolving context ( Zhang et al., 2026g ) , memory ( Zhang et al., 2025a ; Zhang et al., 2026e ; Pan et al., 2026b ) , planning ( Liu et al., 2026b ) , and retrieval ( Lee et al., 2026b ) . At the system level, harness search jointly modifies prompts, tools, and control flow ( Lee et al., 2026a ; Lee et al., 2026c ; Lin et al., 2026 ; Lou et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026d ; Zhang et al., 2026f ) . AutoHarness synthesizes executable support from environmental feedback, while Meta-Harness gives its proposer access to earlier source code, scores, and execution traces ( Lou et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026c ) . Such access preserves evidence that a single scalar score or compressed reflection can omit. Online adaptation extends this process to deployment streams and test-time feedback ( Liu et al., 2026c ; Nie et al., 2026b ; Pan et al., 2026a ) ; population search and reusable repositories retain alternative designs for subsequent exploration ( Zhang et al., 2026h ; Nie et al., 2026a ; Luo et al., 2026b ) . The Darwin Gödel Machine similarly grows an archive of self-modifying agents, allowing earlier branches to become stepping stones for later improvements ( Zhang et al., 2025c ) . Together, these approaches expand the search target from isolated modules to complete execution systems. They also motivate preserving design diversity and execution history, which CoEvo-RSI connects to a corresponding archive of model checkpoints.

sections.heading: Recursive Model Improvement.
sections.text: Model self-improvement converts generated experience into persistent changes in the policy. Three learning loops are particularly relevant. (i) Curricula adapt the source and difficulty of training problems to the learner, including self-play, tool-oriented task generation, and search-agent training without externally supplied demonstrations ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; Acikgoz et al., 2026 ; Sundaram et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026a ; Yang et al., 2026b ; Yue et al., 2026 ) . The resulting feedback loop changes which experiences the model encounters as its competence develops. (ii) Supervision turns demonstrations, privileged feedback, or the model’s own improved behavior into self-distillation targets ( Zhao et al., 2026a ; Shenfeld et al., 2026 ; Hübotter et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Lu et al., 2026b ) . On-policy variants address the learner’s current behavior, making the distribution of generated trajectories central to what can be learned. (iii) Experience reuse extracts reusable skills and transfers their guidance into model behavior ( Xia et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026c ; Lu et al., 2026c ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026c ) . For example, SkillRL jointly evolves a hierarchical skill library and the agent policy, linking experience abstraction with subsequent reinforcement learning ( Xia et al., 2026 ) . These mechanisms improve the agent’s intrinsic capabilities, while the harness determines which tools, observations, and execution constraints appear in its training trajectories. This dependence motivates choosing model initialization and adaptation in relation to the harness that will actually execute the policy.

sections.heading: Model–Harness Co-Evolution.
sections.text: Joint adaptation closes the loop between the environment presented to a policy and the behavior learned under that environment. One line couples (i) context and weights through prompt optimization, continual adaptation, and the transfer of contextual guidance into parameters ( Lu et al., 2026a ; Tiwari et al., 2026 ; Tu et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026b ) . A second line couples (ii) executable harnesses and policies , extending adaptation to the tools, memory, middleware, and control flow used during rollout ( Chen et al., 2026b ; Chen et al., 2026c ; Chen et al., 2026d ; Kim et al., 2026 ; Qi et al., 2026 ; Qu et al., 2026 ; Hebbar et al., 2026 ; Karten et al., 2026 ; Mao et al., 2026 ; TaoLive AIGC LLM Team et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026b ) . HarnessForge combines fault-guided harness tailoring with harness-conditioned policy alignment ( Chen et al., 2026b ) . Co-Harness alternates validated harness patches with fine-tuning on trajectories generated by the improved scaffold ( Chen et al., 2026d ) , while WHALE alternates rejection-sampling fine-tuning with executable harness search ( Kim et al., 2026 ) . A third line brings (iii) execution and editing into a shared learning process, allowing policies to participate in the evolution of their own support ( Luo et al., 2026a ; Shi et al., 2026 ) . These methods establish the value of adapting both sides and expose a common dependency: a harness update changes the execution requirements, and a model update changes which harnesses are effective. CoEvo-RSI makes bidirectional historical inheritance an explicit decision within this loop. Harness editors choose historical starting designs, and model inheritance independently selects or merges archived checkpoints for the resulting requirements. This enables recovery of useful earlier capabilities without tying model initialization to the latest generation or the harness’s parent branch. Appendix D compares the inheritance procedures of representative frameworks.

sections.heading: 3  Method
sections.text: CoEvo-RSI ( Figure 3 ) realizes model–harness co-evolution through bidirectional historical inheritance . An autonomous meta-agent coordinates two complementary decisions: harness editors select and develop historical designs, and model inheritance selects or merges checkpoints for the resulting execution requirements. Evaluation, model adaptation, and promotion turn these inherited components into the next agent, whose outcomes enrich the evolutionary archive. Figure 3 : Overview of CoEvo-RSI . Left: The Curator draws on archived designs, checkpoints, and outcomes to guide evolution. Center: Harness editors choose historical harness bases; checkpoint selection or merging supplies the paired models. Right: Each round evaluates candidate pairs, tracks TIMR, adapts the selected model to its harness, and promotes improvements by validation performance. Outcomes return to the archive.

sections.heading: Evaluation benchmarks.
sections.text: To test whether co-evolution generalizes beyond a single harness design, we evaluate CoEvo-RSI on three domains that demand different harness capabilities: long-trajectory reasoning, policy-constrained tool use, and structured device control. ❶ Failure attribution identifies the responsible agent (Who) and the decisive error step (When) in multi-agent trajectories. We hold out 200 TracerTraj ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) instances for validation during evolution, leaving 3,400 single-error training instances drawn from the remaining TracerTraj data, CORRECT-Error ( Yu et al., 2026a ) , AFTraj ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) , and self-constructed trajectories. The Hand and Algo. subsets of Who&When ( Zhang et al., 2025d ) , Who&When Pro ( Liu et al., 2026a ) , and TraceElephant ( Chen et al., 2026a ) are reserved for out-of-distribution (OOD) testing. ❷ Role-aware text-to-SQL requires generating SQL only when the user’s role authorizes every referenced table and column, and refusing otherwise. We use the Spider subset of the RBAC benchmark ( Fei et al., 2026 ) with its official split and its BIRD subset as an OOD test without any training. ❸ Smart-home instruction following maps instructions to device operations and rejects infeasible ones. We use the valid (VM) and invalid (IM) multi-device subsets of HomeBench ( Li et al., 2025 ) with official splits. Scope: affordable domain specialization We deliberately choose specialized benchmarks because CoEvo-RSI targets compact agents for vertical applications. Examples include lightweight failure-attribution evaluators for large-scale RL training, local smart-home controllers, and enterprise website assistants operating under strict database-access permissions. Our scope is to rapidly optimize reliable, affordable model–harness pairs that deliver domain-specific performance competitive with much larger models.

sections.heading: Baselines.

sections.heading: Implementation.
sections.text: We evolve Qwen3.5-9B ( Qwen Team, 2026 ) from a hand-written initial harness, using DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (high reasoning effort) in Codex ( OpenAI, 2025 ) as the meta-agent. Each run has ten rounds with 𝐊 = 8 \mathbf{K}{=}8 harness candidates per round. The selected Qwen3.5-9B checkpoint samples up to three trajectories per training task under its paired harness at temperature 1, stopping at the first verifier-accepted one. The accepted trajectories are used for one epoch of full-parameter SFT (learning rate 5e-6, batch size 8) on four H100 GPUs. Full data, hyperparameter, baseline, and prompt details are in Appendices A and E .

sections.heading: Failure attribution.
sections.text: We first examine whether co-evolving a small model with its harness can outperform much larger models and single-sided evolution. Table 1 compares the co-evolved 9B agent with all four baseline families. On Who&When Hand, CoEvo-RSI reaches 68.39% Who and 29.31% When accuracy, ahead of the strongest harness-enhanced system FALAT + MiniMax-2.5 (66.30% and 25.90%). On Who&When Algo., it obtains 62.17% Who and 44.71% When accuracy, compared with the strongest baseline scores of 68.25% and 47.62%, respectively. On the other OOD benchmarks, CoEvo-RSI attains 69.43% Who accuracy on Who&When Pro, above Qwen3.8-Max (65.03%), and 70.78% on TraceElephant, 14.16 points above DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 (56.62%). Single-sided evolution falls short: Self-Harness trails CoEvo-RSI by 11.49 Who points on Who&When Hand, and on TraceElephant both harness evolution baselines drop below 10% When accuracy while CoEvo-RSI retains 28.92%; the RL baselines trained under the initial harness likewise trail CoEvo-RSI in Who accuracy on every benchmark, although they attain higher When accuracy on Who&When Pro and TraceElephant. Figure 4 shows how these gains accumulate: over ten rounds, AA improves by 11.11 points and SA by 5.55 points while TIMR stays at or below 0.22%. The strongest gains appear on Who&When Hand and in agent attribution on Who&When Pro and TraceElephant, showing the task-dependent benefits of model–harness alignment. sections.heading: Role-aware text-to-SQL.
sections.text: We next examine access control and query execution under co-evolution. Table 2 compares CoEvo-RSI with direct LLMs and general-purpose coding harnesses. On Spider, CoEvo-RSI achieves the best Safe-EX (80.85%), Safe-Deny (96.64%), and violation rate (1.57%), surpassing Pi + MiniMax-M3 (80.26%, 96.33%, and 1.72%). Figure 5 traces these gains: the harness successively acquires evidence checking, reference-level authorization, and verification with repair, raising Safe-EX from 77.09% to 80.85% and cutting the violation rate from 2.00% to 1.57%, a 21.5% relative reduction. On the OOD BIRD subset, its Safe-EX is close to GLM-5.3 (60.15% vs. 60.90%), alongside the highest Safe-Deny (91.26%), the lowest violation rate (5.65%), and the second-best AC-F1 (90.24%). These results indicate promising cross-database transfer for a 9B model. The safety–utility balance may partly reflect more conservative refusal, which can improve policy compliance while limiting successful execution of authorized queries. Across the run, Safe-EX rises from 77.09% to 80.85%, while violation rate falls from 2.00% to 1.57%, a 21.5% relative reduction.

sections.heading: Smart-home instruction following.
sections.text: Finally, we examine whether co-evolution transfers to structured device control. Table 3 compares CoEvo-RSI with direct LLMs on two multi-device subsets. On valid instructions (VM), CoEvo-RSI achieves the best success rate (75.51%) and F1 (89.23%), ahead of DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 (75.10% and 89.18%). On invalid instructions (IM), it ties for the best success rate (84.54%) and obtains the highest F1 (91.80%). Thus, the co-evolved agent both executes feasible operations and rejects infeasible ones at the level of much larger models. Tables 1 , 2 and 3 show that mismatch-aware co-evolution brings a compact agent close to frontier models on several domain-specific metrics. We view this as a practical form of RSI: an agent directs data generation, model selection, and training to produce stronger models. The evolved model–harness pair is nevertheless tailored to its task family: strong performance on held-out same-domain data, kept strictly separate from evolution, does not imply transfer to unrelated domains. As discussed before Our scope is to maximize a compact agent’s performance within a chosen domain, a practically valuable goal distinct from the broader RSI ambition of autonomous improvement across all domains.

sections.heading: 4.3  Ablation Study
sections.text: We compare full CoEvo-RSI with three variants over ten rounds on Who&When Algo. ( Figure 4 ): Harness-only evolves the harness with a frozen model; Model-only trains under the initial harness; and Latest-only co-evolves both using only the latest generation. ❶ Joint evolution. Harness-only has lower SA than full CoEvo-RSI in every round and TIMR above 1% in eight of ten rounds, versus at most 0.22% for full CoEvo-RSI . Model-only maintains near-zero TIMR with SA at most 35%, indicating that interface compatibility alone is insufficient for task success. ❷ Historical reuse. Latest-only regresses at round 4 and finishes with the lowest SA. Full CoEvo-RSI recovers from its round-4 dip, reusing round-4 weights with new harnesses at rounds 6 and 8 to reach 61.11% and 61.90% AA. Together, these results support complementary roles for bidirectional inheritance and historical reuse in task performance, interface compatibility, and recovery.

AA stays between 45.11% and 52.17%, SA between 28.80% and 37.50%, and TIMR at or below 0.12% for every 𝐊 \mathbf{K} . These results support the robustness of CoEvo-RSI across the tested candidate budgets. We also examine inference cost–accuracy trade-offs in Figure 7 . sections.heading: Cost Analysis.
sections.text: We analyze training cost and inference cost separately. ❶ Training cost. Across the three-round co-evolution runs in Figure 6 (d–f), API expenditure ranges from $2.06 to $3.69. All runs finish within a day (17.48–20.71 hours), with evaluation taking 4.54–6.11 hours. Our default 𝐊 = 8 \mathbf{K}{=}8 achieves the shortest run span of 17.48 hours at an API cost of $2.72. We also compare training rollout budgets ( Table 8 ): across ten rounds, CoEvo-RSI costs fewer rollout budgets than GRPO/GSPO and achieves higher agent accuracy on all four failure-attribution benchmarks ( Table 1 ). ❷ Inference cost. Figure 7 plots Who accuracy on Who&When Hand and Safe-EX on RBAC Spider against the API cost of a full evaluation pass, which for Who&When covers both the Hand and Algo. subsets. On Who&When Hand, CoEvo-RSI reaches 68.39% at $0.16, compared with 60.34% at $3.55 for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, a gain of 8.05 points at 22 × 22\times lower cost. On RBAC Spider, it exceeds the strongest baseline, Pi + MiniMax-M3, by 0.59 Safe-EX points at 38 × 38\times lower cost.

sections.text: Figure 8 pairs every selected harness with every checkpoint from the RBAC run. Only the lower triangle reflects real choices, since round i i can pair 𝐇 i \mathbf{H}_{i} only with checkpoints up to M i \mathrm{M}_{i} . ❶ A growing archive improves interface compatibility. As candidates grow from one to ten checkpoints, the selected pairs move toward low TIMR in the bottom-right corner (mean normalized TIMR from about 0.72 in rounds 1–3 to 0.13 in rounds 6–10), and in seven of ten rounds the selected checkpoint is the lowest-TIMR one available. ❷ Inheritance reaches back into the archive. Five rounds re-select existing weights, and every later derived checkpoint merges with the round-3 checkpoint. Round 10 reuses that checkpoint: with high TIMR under harnesses 4–9 (0.54–1.00), it has the lowest TIMR under the final harness (0.02) and attains the best Safe-EX of the run (80.85%). Interface compatibility is pair-specific; latest-only inheritance misses such pairs.

sections.heading: 5  Conclusion
sections.text: We presented CoEvo-RSI , a bi-level framework that addresses the brain–body mismatch problem in model–harness co-evolution through agent-driven, bidirectional historical inheritance. A shared evolutionary archive and execution feedback guide harness development from historical designs, model checkpoint selection or merging, and subsequent adaptation under the selected harness. Using only SFT on its own rejection-sampled trajectories, CoEvo-RSI makes a compact task model competitive with larger models across multi-agent failure attribution, role-aware text-to-SQL, and smart-home instruction following. Together, these findings highlight brain–body alignment as a central consideration for self-improving agents and bidirectional historical inheritance as a practical route to evolving execution scaffolds (body) and intrinsic capabilities (brain) together.

sections.heading: Appendix A Experimental Details
sections.text: This section details the benchmarks, data, initial harnesses, and hyperparameters behind Section 4.1 . In every domain, training, validation, and test sets are disjoint at the level of sample IDs, tasks, and trajectories. The same validation set 𝐕 \mathbf{V} guides harness and checkpoint selection and promotion during evolution; test sets are reserved for performance reporting. For failure attribution, all 200 validation instances are held out from TracerTraj and removed from the training pool ( Section A.2 ).

sections.heading: Evolution.
sections.text: All domains run ten rounds of co-evolution with 𝐊 = 8 \mathbf{K}{=}8 harness candidates per round. The candidate-sensitivity study in Section 4.4 is the exception and uses three rounds. The meta-agent is DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with high reasoning effort, running inside Codex . In each round, the meta-agent receives validation rollouts of the incumbent model–harness pair. Each editor browses the historical archive, selects an inheritance base, and develops a copy of that harness using the execution evidence and reusable historical designs. The prompt it receives is listed in Appendix E . Each candidate is then evaluated on the full validation set. Candidates are compared using the domain-specific objectives in Table 4 .

sections.heading: Task model and rollout.
sections.text: The task model is Qwen3.5-9B ( Qwen Team, 2026 ) with thinking enabled at high reasoning effort. It is served with vLLM and sampled with temperature 1.0 1.0 , top- p p 0.95 0.95 , and top- k k 20 20 . Per-domain generation budgets, context lengths, and turn limits appear in Table 4 .

sections.heading: Model training.
sections.text: For each training task, the selected model θ ¯ t \bar{\theta}_{t} samples up to three trajectories under its paired harness 𝐇 ¯ t \bar{\mathbf{H}}_{t} , stopping at the first verifier-accepted one. These accepted trajectories, together with selected high-quality accepted trajectories replayed from earlier rounds, are used for one epoch of full-parameter SFT of the same model with ms-swift ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) . Training uses AdamW with learning rate 5 × 10 − 6 5\times 10^{-6} , a cosine schedule with 3% warmup, a per-device batch size of 1, and 4 gradient-accumulation steps. It runs on four H100 GPUs with DeepSpeed ZeRO-3, bf16, and gradient checkpointing. The global batch size is 8 in all domains, and long-context domains additionally use sequence parallelism of size 2. sections.text: Given the full log of a failed multi-agent run, the system must name the agent responsible for the failure (Who) and the decisive step at which the failure becomes unrecoverable (When).

sections.heading: Training and validation data.
sections.text: Training instances come from TracerTraj ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) , CORRECT-Error ( Yu et al., 2026a ) , AFTraj ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) , and a small set of trajectories we construct ourselves. We keep only trajectories that contain a single error, use dense one-based step indices, and have a responsible agent consistent with the decisive step. Of the 1,818 filtered TracerTraj instances, 200 are held out for validation and the remaining 1,618 are retained for training. Together with 1,230 CORRECT-Error, 430 AFTraj, and 122 self-constructed instances, this gives 3,400 training instances. The 200-instance TracerTraj validation set guides candidate and checkpoint selection and promotion. The source studies explicitly document evaluation-data isolation in their respective protocols ( Zhang et al., 2025b ; Yu et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) . We further rigorously checked our training data against the held-out TracerTraj validation set, Who&When Hand, Who&When Algo., Who&When Pro, and TraceElephant. These checks confirmed separation at the sample-ID and task levels and found no identical or highly similar trajectories across training and evaluation.

sections.heading: Metrics.
sections.text: Agent accuracy (AA, reported as Who) is the fraction of instances whose predicted responsible agent matches the annotation. Step accuracy (SA, reported as When) is the fraction whose predicted decisive step matches the annotated step exactly. The harness requires the model to answer through a structured final_answer tool, so predictions are parsed and scored by exact match against the ground truth without an LLM judge. Results are reported separately for each subset.

sections.heading: Initial harness.
sections.text: The hand-written harness exposes the trajectory summary-first: the model initially sees only per-step metadata such as step IDs and agent names. It must call inspect to read the full content of a step, and it submits the agent and step through final_answer . Ground-truth labels are never exposed, and the episode is limited to 20 turns.

sections.heading: Task.
sections.text: Each instance pairs a natural-language question over a database with a user role whose column- and operation-level access policy is given. A request is authorized only if every table, column, and operation it needs is covered by the role’s policy ( Fei et al., 2026 ) . For authorized requests, the system must return SQL that executes to the reference result. Otherwise, it must refuse.

sections.heading: Initial harness.
sections.text: The hand-written harness first applies deterministic rule routing, which links the question to schema columns and checks them against the role policy. When the rules are not confident, it falls back to a multi-turn LLM agent with two tools: test_sql executes a query on the database and returns rows or an error, and final_answer submits the access decision together with SQL when access is granted. The agent is limited to 10 turns.

sections.heading: Task.
sections.text: Each HomeBench ( Li et al., 2025 ) query bundles 2 to 10 sub-instructions for devices in a simulated home. The system must emit one device command per feasible sub-instruction and an error for each infeasible one, such as a missing device or an unsupported operation. We use the VM and IM subsets, which contain only valid and only invalid multi-device queries, respectively.

sections.heading: Metrics.
sections.text: Success is the exact match between the predicted and reference command multisets, including error outputs. F1 is the micro-averaged command-level F1 under the same official counting. Both are computed with the official scorer.

sections.heading: Initial harness.
sections.text: The hand-written harness gives the model a compact index of rooms and devices together with four official in-context examples, and the meta-agent may also edit these examples. Detailed device states and method signatures are available only through the read-only tools inspect_home and list_methods , and the model submits its commands through final_answer . The episode is limited to 20 turns.

sections.heading: Harness evolution.
sections.text: We run Meta-Harness ( Lee et al., 2026c ) and Self-Harness ( Zhang et al., 2026d ) from their official implementations and add a failure attribution domain adapter for each. Both start from the same task model (Qwen3.5-9B), the same hand-written initial harness, and the same 200 held-out TracerTraj validation instances as CoEvo-RSI . Each runs for ten rounds. The task-model weights remain frozen throughout harness evolution. Both baselines use the same meta-agent LLM and settings as CoEvo-RSI , namely DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with high reasoning effort, and each keeps its officially recommended proposer workflow. Meta-Harness drives the LLM through Codex and proposes eight candidates per round. Self-Harness uses its native multi-proposer workflow, which calls the LLM directly without a coding agent, and explores eight candidates per round. Each candidate in both baselines is evaluated twice on the validation set.

sections.text: GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) and GSPO ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) train Qwen3.5-9B under the initial harness on the same 3,400 training instances with verl ( Sheng et al., 2024 ) . The two runs share all settings except the policy loss ( Table 9 ). Both use group-normalized advantages and no KL penalty.

sections.heading: Diagnostic scope.
sections.text: TIMR ( Equation 5 ) measures the frequency of observable interface violations within a model–harness pair: calls to unavailable tools, interface-contract violations, and malformed outputs. These events expose a concrete aspect of brain–body mismatch at the execution boundary and can be checked directly from traces. Their low verification cost makes TIMR useful for diagnosing candidate pairs during evolution. The broader problem definition also covers learned capabilities that a harness underuses or constrains. Such cases can produce valid tool calls throughout an unsuccessful trajectory; assessing them requires task outcomes and examination of the information and actions the harness makes available. TIMR therefore provides a focused operational view of interface compatibility within this broader evaluation. Raw TIMR lies in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] ( 0 0 – 100 % 100\% ); Figure 8 uses global min–max scaling across all harness–checkpoint pairs to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] .

sections.heading: Relationship to task performance.
sections.text: Task success depends jointly on interface use, reasoning, access to relevant evidence, and the execution workflow. The ablations in Figure 4 illustrate these distinct factors: Model-only maintains near-zero TIMR with step accuracy at most 35%, whereas Harness-only has TIMR above 1% in eight of ten rounds and lower step accuracy than full CoEvo-RSI in every round. Full CoEvo-RSI keeps TIMR at or below 0.22% while improving task performance. These observations support using TIMR together with task scores to distinguish execution friction from other performance bottlenecks. They provide diagnostic evidence; attributing a performance gain specifically to lower TIMR would require controlled interventions that isolate interface behavior from changes in reasoning, information access, and execution budget.

sections.heading: Role in co-evolution.
sections.text: CoEvo-RSI reads TIMR alongside task performance when proposing checkpoint selections or merges, and uses validation task scores to select and promote model–harness pairs ( Equations 12 and 13 ). A low TIMR identifies a pair whose observed interactions largely satisfy the harness’s interface requirements; task evaluation establishes how effectively that pair solves the intended problems. This division gives TIMR a practical role as an inexpensive diagnostic signal, with the value of an evolutionary update assessed through downstream performance.

sections.heading: Appendix C Interpreting Comparisons with Frontier Models
sections.text: Our evaluation asks how far co-evolution can bring a compact task model toward frontier-level performance in a given domain. The compared models start from markedly different capability levels: on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3.2, Qwen3.5-9B (Reasoning) scores 11, compared with 36 for DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 (Max) and 45 for GLM-5.3 (Max) ( Artificial Analysis, 2026a ; Artificial Analysis, 2026b ; Artificial Analysis, 2026c ) . These independent measurements contextualize the capability gap behind our task comparisons. Against this background, approaching or matching frontier systems on several demanding tasks is a substantive outcome for a 9B model. For example, CoEvo-RSI achieves 95.51% Spider AC-F1 against 95.85% for the strongest system on this metric, Pi + MiniMax-M3 ( Table 2 ), and 75.51% HomeBench VM success against 75.10% for DeepSeek-V4-Pro ( Table 3 ). Such proximity remains meaningful when individual metric rankings vary across benchmarks. All SFT supervision comes from Qwen3.5-9B’s own verifier-accepted trajectories, generated by the selected checkpoint or, through replay, by earlier checkpoints and retained through rejection sampling ( Section A.1 ). The meta-agent guides harness evolution and checkpoint inheritance; model training consolidates the 9B task model’s successful execution experience. We view the resulting competitiveness as evidence of how much useful capability can be elicited and consolidated from a compact model through coordinated model–harness evolution.

sections.heading: Positioning: affordable domain specialization.
sections.text: As frontier models advance, a complementary deployment need is to make compact models effective within a well-defined domain. We position CoEvo-RSI as a tool for this need, particularly for frequent agent calls where cost and response-time budgets shape system design. Potential applications include device manufacturers integrating smart-home control and RL systems requiring failure-attribution feedback on repeated agent rollouts. These needs motivate our three benchmark domains: smart-home instruction following for device execution, multi-agent failure attribution for automated diagnosis, and role-aware text-to-SQL for policy-constrained data access. Each tests task-specific behavior under concrete operational requirements. The results support this practical motivation: CoEvo-RSI achieves 68.39% agent accuracy on Who&When Hand versus 60.34% for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Under the API pricing in Figure 7 , their full evaluation passes over Hand and Algo. cost $0.16 and $3.55, respectively, approximately 22 × 22\times lower for CoEvo-RSI . Together with the close Spider and HomeBench results above, this demonstrates the value of specialization for delivering competitive task performance at low recurring cost. Small differences on individual metrics can be acceptable when the resulting agent meets an application’s quality requirements and operating budget. Our aim is to give practitioners an affordable model–harness pair optimized for the tasks they repeatedly need to solve.

sections.heading: Appendix E Meta-Agent Prompts
sections.text: The prompt given to the meta-agent in each round has two parts. The first is a shared skeleton that is identical across domains (Prompt A) and fixes the evidence discipline, workflow, and permission boundary. The second is a domain direction (Prompts B–D) that is inserted at the {domain direction} slot and states the domain’s metrics, interface contract, and leakage constraints. Placeholders in braces are filled with run-specific values. The prompts specify the shared evolution workflow and domain-specific instructions, with file paths represented by placeholders. Prompt A: Shared Skeleton shared across all domains You are the CoEvo-RSI meta-agent. Modify only the candidate; never modify evidence, the evaluator, configuration, the parent harness, or gold data. Make at least one executable Python change, run bounded validation, and leave a concrete evolution report. Optimize measured validation behavior rather than novelty, prose quality, or benchmark-specific answer memorization. Incumbent harness: {incumbent harness} Historical archive: {harnesses, provenance, and outcomes} Evidence: {validation rollouts of the incumbent} Objective: {round instruction} Domain direction: {domain direction, see Prompts B--D} Evidence discipline: - Aggregate metadata locally and inspect only a bounded representative sample. - Never dump the complete evidence or complete rollout messages into context. - Use per-sample evaluation metrics to compare successful controls with failures. - Classify failures as harness-addressable, model-capability-limited, or external/data. Headline metrics (in selection priority order): - safe_ex: correct SQL on allowed samples / all allowed samples (primary gate) - ac_f1: access-control F1 (primary gate) - safe_deny: correct refusal rate on denied samples - violation_rate: security breach rate (lower is better) - over_refusal_rate: unnecessary refusal rate (lower is better) - llm_rate: fraction of samples that invoke the LLM (lower is better) - rule_rate / rule_accuracy: coverage and correctness of rule decisions Selection: a child must not regress safe_ex or ac_f1 (tolerance 0.01), then must improve at least one of safe_ex, ac_f1, or llm_rate. The LLM receives two tools: test_sql(sql) executes SQL against the sample database and returns rows or an error; final_answer(access_granted, sql) submits the authorization decision with optional SQL. Abstract Model–harness co-evolution has emerged as a prominent paradigm for recursive self-improving (RSI) agents, jointly evolving their execution scaffolds and intrinsic capabilities. We study the persistent yet often overlooked brain–body mismatch problem in this paradigm, where an evolving harness (body) demands behaviors its model (brain) has not learned or restricts capabilities it already possesses. We introduce CoEvo-RSI , a RSI framework that advances model–harness co-evolution through agent-driven, bidirectional historical inheritance. Drawing on a shared evolutionary archive and execution feedback, a meta-agent coordinates harness development from historical designs with model checkpoint selection or merging and subsequent adaptation under the selected harness, aligning inherited capabilities with evolving execution requirements to reduce brain–body mismatch. Using only supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on its own rejection-sampled trajectories, CoEvo-RSI makes Qwen3.5-9B competitive with larger models across diverse vertical applications, including multi-agent failure attribution, role-aware text-to-SQL, and smart-home instruction following. It surpasses DeepSeek-V4-Pro on TraceElephant ( + 14.16 +14.16 agent accuracy) and GLM-5.3 on HomeBench VM ( + 4.90 +4.90 success rate), underscoring the need for brain–body alignment and the potential of bidirectional historical inheritance to advance agent co-evolution. Agent Failure Attribution (I) and (II) report Who accuracy (correct identification of the responsible agent) on Who&When Hand and TraceElephant, respectively. Role-aware SQL reports safe execution accuracy (Safe-EX) on RBAC Spider; Household Agent reports success rate on HomeBench’s valid multi-device instructions (VM). Dashed arrows trace the improvement from the base model to CoEvo-RSI . 1 Introduction An agent’s capabilities depend jointly on its brain —the language model that reasons and selects actions—and its body —the harness that defines its tool interfaces, action space, memory, and execution workflow ( Lou et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026c ) . Accordingly, progress has followed two complementary directions. Model training improves the agent’s learned policy through supervised learning, reinforcement learning, and self-distillation ( Xia et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026b ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . Harness optimization improves the surrounding system with the model fixed, through iterative modification of prompts, tools, and control flow guided by execution feedback ( Lou et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026 ) , or population-based evolution that generates, evaluates, and recombines competing harness designs ( Lee et al., 2026c ; Zhang et al., 2026h ) . These directions meet in model–harness co-evolution , where model training and harness optimization jointly adapt an agent to its task domain ( Chen et al., 2026c ; Luo et al., 2026a ) . Recent systems demonstrate the promise of this approach across tool use, mathematical reasoning, search-based question answering, and chess ( Chen et al., 2026b ; Chen et al., 2026d ; Kim et al., 2026 ) . A co-evolution round couples harness evolution with model adaptation. Starting from a model–harness pair ( 𝐇 t , θ t ) (\mathbf{H}_{t},\theta_{t}) , execution feedback 𝐅 t \mathbf{F}_{t} guides changes to the harness, whose requirements in turn shape the model’s next adaptation ( Chen et al., 2026d ) . As either component evolves, the harness’s execution requirements and the model’s learned capabilities can drift apart. In this setting, we first identify and formalize the brain–body mismatch problem : Problem Definition During model–harness co-evolution, a pair ( 𝐇 t , θ t ) (\mathbf{H}_{t},\theta_{t}) exhibits brain–body mismatch when the behaviors required by 𝐇 t \mathbf{H}_{t} diverge from those learned by θ t \theta_{t} , or when 𝐇 t \mathbf{H}_{t} restricts the use of capabilities already present in θ t \theta_{t} . The problem is to maintain their compatibility through successive rounds of harness-model co-adaptation. Figure 2 : Brain–body alignment in model–harness co-evolution. Left: Historical harnesses and checkpoints are recombined and adapted to resolve interface mismatch. Right: Step accuracy versus Turn-level Interface Mismatch Rate (TIMR; Section 3.1 ) for ten evolved versions per method, from a three-round run evaluated on the Who&When test benchmark. In plain terms, the model may struggle to operate its harness, and the harness may underuse its model’s abilities ( Figure 2 ). Consider two concrete examples. ❶ Interface mismatch. The model emits XML tool calls, while the evolved harness expects JSON, causing otherwise correct calls to be rejected. ❷ Capability mismatch. The harness introduces an active context management tool for deciding what information to retain, summarize, or discard. A model unfamiliar with these operations may use it poorly; a historical checkpoint θ i \theta_{i} already possesses the relevant capabilities and provides a suitable starting point for adaptation. On the harness side, a historical design 𝐇 j \mathbf{H}_{j} can supply an execution workflow suited to the model’s capabilities. These examples motivate selecting predecessors whose inherited behaviors and structures support further evolution. To address this challenge, we propose CoEvo-RSI , a framework for model–harness co-evolution through bidirectional historical inheritance . Its evolutionary archive 𝐀 < t \mathbf{A}_{<t} records earlier harnesses, model checkpoints, their development histories, and execution outcomes. Each round begins with feedback from the current pair. A Curator organizes this evidence, and harness editors browse the archive, choose their own historical starting designs, and develop offspring harnesses. For each offspring, the framework selects or merges historical checkpoints to form candidate model–harness pairs. Evaluation identifies a promising pair for model adaptation under its harness, and validation determines which pair advances to the next round. The resulting designs, checkpoints, and outcomes extend the archive. This agent-driven inheritance connects the two sides of evolution: harness design draws on accumulated structural experience, while model initialization draws on capabilities suited to the emerging harness. Their coordination makes brain–body alignment the organizing principle of the evolutionary process. Our contributions are: • Problem Formalization. We formalize brain–body mismatch in model–harness co-evolution and introduce the turn-level interface mismatch rate (TIMR) as an inexpensive diagnostic signal for observable interface violations. • Method Design. We propose CoEvo-RSI , which combines an evolutionary archive with bidirectional historical inheritance. Harness editors select historical starting designs, and model inheritance selects or merges checkpoints to support adaptation under the evolved harness. • Empirical Evaluation. We evaluate CoEvo-RSI across multi-agent failure attribution, home care, and SQL tasks, with co-evolved Qwen3.5-9B outperforming Qwen3.8-Max on Who&When Pro ( + 4.40 +4.40 agent acc.) and DeepSeek-V4-Pro on TraceElephant ( + 14.16 +14.16 agent acc.). 2 Related Work Self-evolving agents improve through changes to external execution systems, learned model parameters, or both ( Gao et al., 2026 ; Guo et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . We organize the literature around these optimization targets and the reuse of historical components that connects them. Recursive Harness Improvement. Early agent systems established how external organization can improve a model’s behavior: ReAct interleaves reasoning and actions, Reflexion retains verbal feedback across trials, and Voyager accumulates reusable executable skills ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Shinn et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) . Agent–computer interface design further shows how the operations exposed to a model shape its effectiveness ( Yang et al., 2024 ) . Subsequent work turns these hand-designed mechanisms into optimization targets, evolving context ( Zhang et al., 2026g ) , memory ( Zhang et al., 2025a ; Zhang et al., 2026e ; Pan et al., 2026b ) , planning ( Liu et al., 2026b ) , and retrieval ( Lee et al., 2026b ) . At the system level, harness search jointly modifies prompts, tools, and control flow ( Lee et al., 2026a ; Lee et al., 2026c ; Lin et al., 2026 ; Lou et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026d ; Zhang et al., 2026f ) . AutoHarness synthesizes executable support from environmental feedback, while Meta-Harness gives its proposer access to earlier source code, scores, and execution traces ( Lou et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026c ) . Such access preserves evidence that a single scalar score or compressed reflection can omit. Online adaptation extends this process to deployment streams and test-time feedback ( Liu et al., 2026c ; Nie et al., 2026b ; Pan et al., 2026a ) ; population search and reusable repositories retain alternative designs for subsequent exploration ( Zhang et al., 2026h ; Nie et al., 2026a ; Luo et al., 2026b ) . The Darwin Gödel Machine similarly grows an archive of self-modifying agents, allowing earlier branches to become stepping stones for later improvements ( Zhang et al., 2025c ) . Together, these approaches expand the search target from isolated modules to complete execution systems. They also motivate preserving design diversity and execution history, which CoEvo-RSI connects to a corresponding archive of model checkpoints. Recursive Model Improvement. Model self-improvement converts generated experience into persistent changes in the policy. Three learning loops are particularly relevant. (i) Curricula adapt the source and difficulty of training problems to the learner, including self-play, tool-oriented task generation, and search-agent training without externally supplied demonstrations ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; Acikgoz et al., 2026 ; Sundaram et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026a ; Yang et al., 2026b ; Yue et al., 2026 ) . The resulting feedback loop changes which experiences the model encounters as its competence develops. (ii) Supervision turns demonstrations, privileged feedback, or the model’s own improved behavior into self-distillation targets ( Zhao et al., 2026a ; Shenfeld et al., 2026 ; Hübotter et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Lu et al., 2026b ) . On-policy variants address the learner’s current behavior, making the distribution of generated trajectories central to what can be learned. (iii) Experience reuse extracts reusable skills and transfers their guidance into model behavior ( Xia et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026c ; Lu et al., 2026c ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026c ) . For example, SkillRL jointly evolves a hierarchical skill library and the agent policy, linking experience abstraction with subsequent reinforcement learning ( Xia et al., 2026 ) . These mechanisms improve the agent’s intrinsic capabilities, while the harness determines which tools, observations, and execution constraints appear in its training trajectories. This dependence motivates choosing model initialization and adaptation in relation to the harness that will actually execute the policy. Model–Harness Co-Evolution. Joint adaptation closes the loop between the environment presented to a policy and the behavior learned under that environment. One line couples (i) context and weights through prompt optimization, continual adaptation, and the transfer of contextual guidance into parameters ( Lu et al., 2026a ; Tiwari et al., 2026 ; Tu et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026b ) . A second line couples (ii) executable harnesses and policies , extending adaptation to the tools, memory, middleware, and control flow used during rollout ( Chen et al., 2026b ; Chen et al., 2026c ; Chen et al., 2026d ; Kim et al., 2026 ; Qi et al., 2026 ; Qu et al., 2026 ; Hebbar et al., 2026 ; Karten et al., 2026 ; Mao et al., 2026 ; TaoLive AIGC LLM Team et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026b ) . HarnessForge combines fault-guided harness tailoring with harness-conditioned policy alignment ( Chen et al., 2026b ) . Co-Harness alternates validated harness patches with fine-tuning on trajectories generated by the improved scaffold ( Chen et al., 2026d ) , while WHALE alternates rejection-sampling fine-tuning with executable harness search ( Kim et al., 2026 ) . A third line brings (iii) execution and editing into a shared learning process, allowing policies to participate in the evolution of their own support ( Luo et al., 2026a ; Shi et al., 2026 ) . These methods establish the value of adapting both sides and expose a common dependency: a harness update changes the execution requirements, and a model update changes which harnesses are effective. CoEvo-RSI makes bidirectional historical inheritance an explicit decision within this loop. Harness editors choose historical starting designs, and model inheritance independently selects or merges archived checkpoints for the resulting requirements. This enables recovery of useful earlier capabilities without tying model initialization to the latest generation or the harness’s parent branch. A shared evolutionary archive and execution feedback guide harness development from historical designs, model checkpoint selection or merging, and subsequent adaptation under the selected harness. Using only SFT on its own rejection-sampled trajectories, CoEvo-RSI makes a compact task model competitive with larger models across multi-agent failure attribution, role-aware text-to-SQL, and smart-home instruction following. Together, these findings highlight brain–body alignment as a central consideration for self-improving agents and bidirectional historical inheritance as a practical route to evolving execution scaffolds (body) and intrinsic capabilities (brain) together.
